newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Mainland ties seen helping HK Telecom locally, in China.
newsitem.headline: Mainland ties seen helping HK Telecom locally, in China.

text.p: Hongkong Telecom could kill two birds with one stone if it finds the right Chinese partner -- gain access to China's vast market and settle its status after the Hong Kong handover, analysts said on Monday.
Uncertainty surrounding the company's status after Britain hands Hong Kong back to China in mid-1997 has plagued Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd shares.
Investors have fretted that its ties to Britain, through Cable and Wireless Plc would hamper future business.

London's Sunday Telegraph said Hongkong Telecom was likely to pass into Chinese hands, with Cable and Wireless set to slash its 58.6 percent stake to less than 50 percent in return for better access to the Chinese market.
"I think it would bolster confidence in Hongkong Telecom's position post-1997 here in the Hong Kong market," David Gibbons, regional telecoms analyst at HSBC James Capel, said on Monday.
"And it would be seen as opening the door for Hongkong Telecom to participate in a huge and largely untapped China telecoms market," he added.
Hongkong Telecom dismissed the Sunday Telegraph report as "gossip" but investors applauded the prospect, driving the company's shares HK$0.80 higher to close at HK$13.70 on Monday.
"There is a view in the marketplace that they would have some more support for their local business," said Fredson Bowers, director of Asia telecoms research at W.I. Carr.
He said a Chinese partner would probably help the telephone utility in its current negotiations with the Hong Kong government on its international telephone franchise.

"Any revisions to the licence would have to be approved by the JLG (Joint Liason Group) and therefore it would be very beneficial for Hongkong Telecom to have a Chinese shareholder to help smooth that process," said Bowers.
The Sino-British JLG is the forum in which British and Chinese diplomats are hammering out handover details.

"Secondly, the view in the industry is virtually unanimous that within the next 18 months there will be substantially more opportunities for investment in China's telecom industry and having the right shareholder would improve investment prospects," Bowers said.

Gibbons expected the fixed line and cellular phone market in China to triple between 1995 and 2000. "That is 80 million new fixed line and cellular subscribers. It is a very, very big market," he said.
Instead of participating in rather piecemeal investments, analysts said Hongkong Telecom would be able to pursue larger investments in fixed line and cellular networks.
But Hongkong Telecom's prospects would depend on who it linked up with, they added.

"If it is the (China's ) Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications they should get a foothold in the door and it also helps them a lot on the regulatory front," said Johnny Wong, investment analyst at ING Barings.
Gibbons said other candidates could be the People's Liberation Army and China's major utilities companies.

Analysts said a new partner would need to take a significant stake to make a difference. "It is not clear whether 10 percent would really seal a relationship with other parties. But it could be part of a bigger transaction," said Gibbons.

Bowers said Cable and Wireless would also have to reduce its stake substantially. "The sort of levels which have been mooted -- slightly under 50 percent -- I don't think are sufficient. In order to really structurally change the outlook for Hongkong Telecom. Cable and Wireless has to go below 35 percent."
